entry.title: In Water, Clarity doesn’t imply Safety

link.title: In Water, Clarity doesn’t imply Safety

entry.content:
Your Water is Clear doesn’t mean it’s Clean

There are different types of contamination and different levels to contamination. We have the physical, microbiological and chemical contamination.

The physical contamination has to do with color, turbidity- (the amount of suspended particles in your water, say sand, clay, dirts, etc) and taste. The microbiological contamination which is the most paramount concern of a water scientist, refers to the presence of bacteria, protozoa, viruses and helminths. The most uncommon form of contamination is the chemical contamination which is the presence of chemicals like arsenic, copper, mercury in the water. This is mostly due to industrial processes and effluent in the water.

The physical contamination is usually the easiest to deal with and is responsible for the “dirty” look of your water. The muddiness is usually a product of turbidity which can be reduced through sedimentation, that is allowing the water to settle for a certain period of time — natural settlement, or using natural coagulants like moringa seed powder in the water, thoroughly mixing and then settling for a while, or the use of chemical coagulants to speed up the process of coagulation-particles coming together/merging to form bigger particles.

After the process of sedimentation, the water can then be transferred into another bucket or container. You can further treat your water by filtering the water produced from sedimentation. In households, this could be done using cloths especially cotton materials, folding them 4 times to have 16 layers and then placing the cloth on a bucket and sieving the water through the cloth. You can also use bio-sand filters, ceramic candle filters or ceramic filters.

After this process, a large proportion of turbidity is gone, which means your water is now clear. However, this doesn’t mean the water is safe to drink yet.

There are still chances of microbial contamination which are responsible for cholera, diarrhea and other forms of waterborne diseases.

You can treat your water further by disinfecting it, there are several methods to do this at home. You can either use the most popular method of chemical disinfection, Chlorine. You just have to make sure to read the directions on usage and dose which is how many drops or quantity per litres of water depending on whether you bought powdered or liquid form. Some form of microorganisms can however escape this treatment due to the presence of a protective shield called cysts.

Or you can use the most popular traditional method of disinfection- boiling. Most microorganisms cannot survive past the boiling temperature of 100 degrees celsius, which is the point your water starts bubbling. Although, the boiling point depends on the altitude, that is, your position in relation to the sea level, a 100 degrees celsius is safe enough to treat the water. You can then allow the water to cool before transferring to a sealed container with taps to avoid recontamination.

Talking about recontamination, a safe way to avoid this after disinfection is to use the SODIS (Solar Disinfection) method. This means storing your water in PET bottles, and placing them outside on a flat surface for the sun to heat them up and kill or inactivate the microorganisms in your water. Asides the heat, this process makes use of the UV rays from the sun to disinfect your water. However, the duration of the exposure to sun is dependent on the weather, whether it’s sunny or cloudy.

It is free from the risk of recontamination because the water can be drunk directly from the PET bottles. Also, researches have shown that there’s no chemical contamination from exposing the PET bottles to sunlight, so, yes, the water is safe to drink.

Side note: Do not store your water in transparent containers, as this supports the growth of algal blooms in your water as it allows the rays of sunlight to pass through it.

entry.title: Using The Sun to Disinfect Your Drinking Water

link.title: Using The Sun to Disinfect Your Drinking Water

entry.content:
There are different ways of disinfecting(inactivating pathogens) water, chemical and ultraviolet radiation. The disinfection of water through ultraviolet radiation can be artificial radiation which needs electricity and lamps to generate energy or natural energy which uses the sun’s energy for solar disinfection.

Ultraviolet radiation is a type of energy along the electromagnetic spectrum, where different kinds of radiation are defined by their wavelength. Ultraviolet has wavelength in the range of 100–400 nanometer with visible light in the 400–700 nanometer range.

Ranges of UV radiation

· Vacuum UV (Only exists in the vacuum): 100 -200 nm

· UV-C (Deep Ultraviolet): 200–280nm

· UV-B: 280 -315 nm

· UV-A: 315 -400nm

Note: The germicidal peak of UV radiation is at 260nm which is in the UV-C range, hence why most commercial UV systems target this wavelength of 260nm. UV-C is the most effective against bacteria then, protozoa cysts, then, viruses and bacterial spores which need larger dose to inactivate those kinds of pathogens.

A dosage of UV radiation is the product of Intensity of UV radiation * Time.

The typical dose is 400J/m2 at which there would more than 4 log removal of bacteria, almost 4 log removal of rotavirus, but only a little bit more than 1 log removal of Bacillus subtilis spores with e-coli readily removed with even greater log removal than bacteria.

Log Reduction Value is a performance parameter that refers to the number of log units by which a chemical or other contaminants is reduced through treatment.

For example, if a particular sample has 1,000,000 counts of contaminants, a reduction to 100,000 which is a 90% reduction is equivalent to 1 LRV. If it is a 99% reduction, that is the concentration of contaminant is reduced to 10,000 count, the log removal is 2.

Therefore, 4 log removal of bacteria can be visualized as reducing a 100,000 count of bacteria to 10.

UV-C is quite effective in water treatment, has no impact on pH. However, turbidity could shield particles and a higher dose is required at low temperatures. UV-C can be generated using lamps which requires electricity, e.g. low-pressure mercury lamps (with 254nm), medium-pressure lamps (200–440nm) and LED lamps at a particular wavelength at a lower cost than mercury lamps. However this is mostly used in medium-high income countries, for low-income countries, a cost-effective alternative is the solar disinfection.

Solar Disinfection (SODIS)

Solar Disinfection (SODIS) works by simply taking a clean plastic (PET) bottle, filling it with water and then lying it on a flat surface, maybe a rooftop and exposing it to natural sunlight for at least 6 hours, or if it is a cloudy day, for two days. After this exposure, the water is safe to drink. Over 20 countries, 5 million people use this method as a disinfection process for their water treatment.

SODIS doesn’t use UV-C radiation because as the sunlight passes through the atmosphere, all of the UV-C and even about 90% of UV-B is absorbed by the ozone, water vapor, oxygen and carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, but UV-A is less affected by the atmosphere. Therefore, the UV-radiation reaching the earth’s surface is largely composed of UV-A and a bit of UV-B component. So, SODIS works differently from UV-C disinfection and it does so with three main mechanisms.

1. Direct Inactivation: UV-B radiation can still directly inactivate cells. It won’t be much absorbed by the DNA but other components within the cells, like proteins, enzymes can be affected. However, much of the UV-B is removed by PET bottles, so this is just a minor effect.

2. Indirect Inactivation: The UV-A radiation is absorbed by some intermediate species which go on to create reactive oxygen species like hydroxyl radical or hydrogen peroxide, which causes damage to the microbes. This could be internal with these reactive oxygen species (ROS) been generated inside the cell if the cell contains chromophores, which are typically present in bacterial cells or externally through dissolved organic matter or dissolved ion.

3. Heat: If the temperature gets to 60–70oc, it gets to a point of pasteurization, but even at 50oc, heat plays an important role in the effects of radiation.

Factors Influencing the Effect of SODIS

· UV-radiation: The height of sun is important, because the higher the sun, the higher the radiation level and this varies with the time of the day and year.

· Latitude and Altitude: Radiation doesn’t fall equally on the earth and the higher the altitude, the more the radiation with UV levels increasing by about 10% for every 1000 metres.

· Ozone and Ground Reflection: The ozone in the atmosphere reduces UV and can vary spacially, varies over the year, and even across the year.

· Water Column: The depth of the water in the bottle is also important as UV radiation is attenuated (depreciated) by water. Therefore, if the bottle is too large and the water column were too thick, then the UV wouldn’t penetrate to the centre of the bottle.

· Characteristics of Water:

a. Temperature: When water temperature reaches 50oc, there’s a synergy and only about one hour of UV exposure is needed.

b. Turbidity (Measure of suspended particles in water): This negatively affects SODIS and if the turbidity is >30NTU, it is advised to pretreat the water with filtration (passing the water through a clean cloth), or coagulation (Using coagulants such as alum and mixing thoroughly to accumulate particles) and sedimentation (allowing particles to settle before sieving).

Efficacy of SODIS

Protozoa such as Giardia cysts, Cryptosporidium spores are inactivated: 2->4 LRV

Bacteria (3->5 LRV): Salmonella have been found to be more persistent than E.coli and Shigella and Vibrio Cholera are relatively susceptible to ultraviolet radiation.

Viruses (1->5 LRV): Adenovirus is quite resistant to SODIS but also to UV-C radiation, whilst echovirus is relatively easier to disinfect with SODIS.

Concerns Raised About the Exposure Plastic Materials to the Sun for Water Treatment

· Antimony: A chemical used as catalyst in the production of PET, but it only leaches into water at appreciable levels when the water is in contact with the plastic for many weeks or longer or if the temperature exceeds 70oc. However, this doesn’t happen during SODIS treatment since the water is only in the bottle for few days and temperature rarely exceeds 50oc.

· Adipates and Phthalates: These are used as softeners in the production of certain plastics like PVC used in plastic pipes. Although, not particularly toxic, the softeners can present a threat to health if they are consumed in large quantities. Thankfully, these softeners are not used in the production of PET which are used in SODIS, so they can’t leach into the water.

· Aldehydes: These are formed when the plastic is heated in the manufacturing process for PET bottles, however, laboratory investigations have found that the exposure to sun has no effect on the concentrations of aldehydes that could be measured especially for acetaldehydes. However, the concentration of formaldehydes does increase with the length of exposure, but the concentrations remain far below the standard regulatory limit for drinking water. Formaldehydes and Acetaldehydes can be a problem for bottled carbonated water because the higher pressure and lower pH within these bottles can result in aldehydes in stored water. However, the pressure and pH are moderate in SODIS treatment, so these chemicals are not found at levels of concern in SODIS treated water.

· Bisphenol A: A chemical present in some plastic bottles which is suspected to cause breast cancer. However, this is only an issue with polycarbonate bottles and plastics and not in PET bottles used for SODIS.

· Genotoxicity: Mutations in certain plants or protozoa or bacteria cells as a result of exposure to water. Studies have shown that water stored in plastic bottles for long periods like several months, cell mutations could be observed. However, this occurred with or without exposure to UV radiation, so, while it might be an issue for long term storage, it is not directly pertinent to SODIS.

Since SODIS involves neither long storage time nor high temperatures, there has not been any evidence that SODIS introduces any harm or chemicals to treated water.

Advantages of SODIS

· Highly effective, although UV-C is more effective especially against viruses and protozoa.

· The SODIS is inexpensive and simple to operate

· There’s low risk of recontamination with SODIS because the water is typically drunk from the same container where it has been treated.

Challenges of SODIS

· Both UV-C and SODIS are limited to low turbidity waters because particles can shield pathogens from the radiation.

· UV-C requires electricity to run the lamps.

· SODIS is highly dependent on the climate, thus takes significant time.

· Only small volumes of water can be treated at a time in a batch of SODIS treatment.

Introduction to Household Water Treatment and Safe Storage

entry.title: Is Sleep Really Important for the Brain?

link.title: Is Sleep Really Important for the Brain?

entry.content:
While I was taking a course on ‘Learning How to Learn” on Coursera, I learnt that sleep is an integral part of retaining memory, as the diffused mode of learning occurs during sleep. This is when the chunks of knowledge gathered during the focused mode are connected, allowing the brain to further understand and ingrain the knowledge.

Luckily, I had found this dataset from the Statistics course on Udacity. It has the results from a BBC test on memory where you are shown two set of 12 pictures with five minutes breaks in-between, then you take a test where you’re shown different pictures and asked if they were part of the pictures you had seen and which set you saw them in. After the test, you get a result showing your recognition memory score which refers to your ability to remember if you had seen a picture or not, and your temporal memory score which refers to your ability to remember which set you saw the picture in. Students taking the Statistics were told to enter their scores from this test and the number of hours they slept the night before.

The dataset had 4 columns and 9158 rows including the header row. The columns were “Timestamp (the time each student made the entry)”, ”How many hours did you sleep last night?”, “Recognition Score” and “Temporal Memory Score”.

Exploratory Data Analysis (Microsoft Excel)

1. Data Cleaning

a. Removed rows with missing values, using the filter function

b. Removed Timestamp

c. Removed Outliers using IQR (Interquartile Range) Method

d. Removed the rows with Temporal and Recognition scores greater than 100.

e. Change datatypes of Temporal and Recognition Memory Scores to percentage

f. Manually edited the scores that changed to decimals or a product of 100%

2. Descriptive Statistics

a. Used the Data tab- Data Analysis — Descriptive Statistics feature on Excel to produce a table describing the dataset

b. Plotted a histogram for the number of hours spent asleep using defined bin size of 1

c. Due to the low values of sleep duration for 14–24 hours, another histogram was plotted showing hours between 0 and 13

d. Histograms for the Recognition and Temporal memory scores were plotted with a bin size of 10

From the count, we can see that the rows of data has reduced from 9158 to 8778, i.e. 380 rows removed. Since the temporal memory score has the highest SD, it shows that the temporal memory scores are more spread out. This can also be seen as the temporal memory scores has the highest variance. The median shows that 50% of the people sleep for 7 hours, have a score of 92 and 80 for recognition and temporal memory. The mode interprets that the most frequently occurring sleep duration is 7 hours, with 100 and 68 being the most common recognition and temporal memory scores. The values of skewness and kurtosis show that the distributions is negatively skewed (there are more high values) and are leptokurtic (have high peaks) with the distribution of recognition scores having the highest peak. Since, the mean, median and mode for the hours of sleep are very close in values i.e. 6.7, 7, 7, we can say the distribution of the sleep duration is close to being normally distributed. All these can also be seen in the charts below.

1. Regression and Correlation Analysis

a. Plotted a scatter plots of each variable against the other

b. A correlation table was drawn to get an insight of the relationship between the variables.

c. Conducted a regression statistics on the variables

From the plots, a correlation between the scores and the number of hours spent asleep is not obvious, so we would a correlation table to check that later. However, we can see a trend of a line in the scatter plots for the scores which makes it obvious that the scores themselves have a linear relationship.

From the plots, a correlation between the scores and the number of hours spent asleep is not obvious, so we would a correlation table to check that later. However, we can see a trend of a line in the scatter plots for the scores which makes it obvious that the scores themselves have a linear relationship.

This shows that the recognition score and temporal memory score both have low positive correlations with the hours of sleep, with that of the temporal memory score being a little higher. The correlation coefficient value of 0.522 confirms the positive linear relationship (mutual dependence exist) we saw in the scatter plot of the recognition score against the temporal memory score.

Note: This was done after the further data preparation

The R2 values shows that only 0.09% variation in recognition scores can be explained by the variation in hours of sleep, 0.2% of variation in temporal memory scores can be explained by the hours of sleep, and 27% of variation in recognition scores can be explained by the variation in temporal memory scores. The standard error values indicate the average distance of observed values from the predicted values i.e refers to the discrepancy in the regression line

Further Data Preparation

a. Removed the rows of data with hours of sleep greater than 15 (This was due to their low frequency to start with)

b. Grouped the hours of sleep into 3;

i. Below Recommended: 0–5.5 hours

ii. Recommended: 6–10 hours

iii. Above Recommended: 10.5–15.0

c. Plotted a bar chart of memory scores against the hours of sleep

Data Investigation (SPSS)

This investigation is to verify if sleep really plays a role in memory retention.

So, the Null Hypothesis is that the means of the recognition and temporal memory scores are not significantly different for the groups ie

While the alternative hypothesis is that means of the recognition and temporal memory scores are significantly different for the groups (the number of hours of sleep has an effect on the memory scores) i.e

Where µ: Mean

a: Above recommended

b: Below recommended

r: Recommended

a. Excel file was imported into SPSS

b. Conducted another set of descriptive statistics

c. Produced a table of percentiles

d. Produced another correlation table

e. Compared the means to note if there are significant difference between the means

f. Conducted a t-test to compare the means of below recommended and recommended sleep group

g. Conducted a t-test to compare the means of below recommended, recommended and above recommended sleep group. (Had to encode the sleep group to do this)

Results and Discussion

a. Descriptive Statistics

There isn’t much difference in the values of the measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode) and measures of dispersion (standard deviation, variance). However, the range is now 15.0 due to the rows removed. Also the percentiles show the values for people below each percentile, 10% of people sleep for 4.5 hours, have a recognition score of 75% and temporal memory score of 63%.

b. Percentiles

This shows that 5% of people sleep for 0 hours, have 68% and 57% recognition and temporal scores and 95% people sleep for a maximum of 9.5 hours, with 100% and 95% recognition and temporal scores. These shows that more people have higher recognition score compared to temporal memory scores. Also if your temporal memory score is above 95%, you’re in the top 5% as opposed to recognition score where even a 100% recognition score putting you in the top 25%.

c. Correlations

This is consistent with the finding that memory scores are positively correlated with the hours of sleep with temporal memory scores being more highly correlated. This also shows that these correlation is significant at an alpha level of 0.01 with the correlation between temporal memory scores and hours of sleep and recognition score is significant even at an alpha level of 0.001 based on the significance values from the table.

d. Independent Samples T-Test

This shows that at 0.05, 0.01 and even 0.001 alpha level there’s a significant difference between the means of the below recommended and recommended groups for the temporal memory scores judging by the p-values. However, the difference in the means of recognition scores of the sleep groups is significant only at an alpha level of 0.05.

The positive values of Cohen’s d (0.058 and 0.091) indicate that the post-treatment (recommended hours of sleep group) has higher means compared to the pre-treatment (below recommended hours of sleep) for both the recognition score and temporal memory score respectively.

e. Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)

This shows that at a 0.05 and 0.01 alpha level, there is a significant difference in the temporal memory scores depending on the sleep group judging by the significance of .002. Whilst, there’s no significant difference in recognition memory scores at both 0.05 and 0.01 alpha level. This concludes that sleep plays a crucial role in temporal memory which might not necessarily be true for recognition memory score.

Eta-squared also called explanation refers to the proportion of total variation that is due to between-group differences. So, from the table we can infer that only 0.1% of recognition and temporal memory scores can be explained due to the differences in sleep groups. 99.9% remains unexplained.

f. Tukey’s HSD

According to what I learnt from the statistics course, we only use Tukey’s HSD when we have the same sample size for each group, but I wanted to see the representation of results. Also, SPSS gave a disclaimer regarding the group sizes being unequal and Type 1 error (rejecting a null hypothesis when it is actually true) levels not guaranteed.

This shows that only the mean difference between the groups below the recommended sleep hours and those within the recommended hours is significant for temporal memory scores, this interprets as that the two groups are honestly significantly different.

Conclusion

Based on these results we reject the null hypothesis and accept the alternative hypothesis for the relationship between the hours of sleep and the temporal memory scores. However, there is not enough evidence to reject the null hypothesis between the hours of sleep and recognition memory scores, so we fail to reject the null hypothesis. Therefore, it can be concluded that the number of hours you sleep, i.e. sleeping for the recommended duration has a positive effect on your temporal memory, i.e. your ability to remember where and when you saw something. The effect of the hours of sleep on the recognition score could not be proven.

Recommendation

Sleep well

entry.title: Global Burden of Diseases Caused By Unsafe Water

link.title: Global Burden of Diseases Caused By Unsafe Water

entry.content:
Water quality is as important as the availability of water because unsafe water is a non-negligible cause of many diseases. But, did you know that water-borne diseases are not the only classes of disease caused by unsafe water?

I found out recently too, and that reemphasized the need to seek more knowledge, cos how much more do I not know?

Classification of Diseases Caused by Unsafe Water

1. Water-borne Diseases: Caused by directly drinking, ingesting water that has some pathogens in it. Diarrheal diseases caused by different pathogens like Rotavirus, Cholera, Shigella, Cryptosporidiosis, Hepatitis A and E, Polio. The best intervention would be to improve water quality.

2. Water-washed Diseases: Caused by poor hygiene due to lack of water as opposed to direct ingestion. Most water-borne diseases are also water-washed because they can be transmitted through hands and contact with other surfaces, e.g. Trachoma (transmitted by flies) which is the leading cause of preventable blindness, Acute Respiratory Infections which are transmitted through contact with pathogens on hands or other surfaces. These can be prevented by increasing the quantity of water to improve hygiene.

3. Water-based Diseases: Caused by parasites which live part of their life-cycle in water e.g. schistosomiasis (bilharzia) which affects 160million people globally mostly in the Sub-Saharan Africa, and Dracunculiasis (Guinea worm) which used to affect a lot of people but has reduced now. These can be prevented by targeting the aquatic organism host and protecting surface water bodies.

4. Water-related Diseases: Caused by insects which breed in water especially mosquitoes. An example is malaria which affects about 250 million people each year causing about 589,000 deaths, majority of which is once again in the Sub-Saharan Africa and affect children under the age of five. Dengue fever which is growing in numbers and causes explosive outbreaks especially in urban areas is another example. A good control mechanism would be to remove the habitats of the insects.

As at 2012, the global mortality recorded for these common diseases were;

  1. Lower Respiratory Infections (Pneumonia) — 3,051,000
  2. Diarrheal Disease — 1,498,000
  3. Tuberculosis — 935,000
  4. Malaria — 618,000
  5. Measles — 130,000

I can’t be the only one that thought Malaria would have a higher global mortality figure than diarrheal disease, right?

The most important of the Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) diseases and a major contributor of the global burden of diseases is Diarrheal Diseases raking in about 1.5 million deaths per year, causing about 1 in 10 deaths for children less than 5 years i.e. about 1,000 child deaths per day. 56% of these deaths is attributed to inadequate WASH. It is therefore apparent that poor access to basic WASH services have a major impact in global deaths.

However, asides deaths as a burden of diseases, it is important to consider sickness which can greatly reduce the quality of life and this can be done using a metric called Disability Adjusted Life Years (DALYs).

Disability Adjusted Life Years

DALY = YLL + YLD

YLL: Years of Life Lost = Number of Deaths * Standard Life Expectancy at age of death in years

YLD: Years Lost to Disability/ Years Lived with Disability = Number of years you lived with the disability * Disability Weight.

Note: Each disability has a weight dependent on its severity defined by WHO.

Example 1: A person with a life expectancy of 70 years, lives a healthy life through to 70.

Therefore, there is no life lost due to premature death or due to disability.

YLL = 0

YLD = 0

Hence, DALYs = YLL + YLD = 0 years

Example 2: Life Expectancy = 80 years

Accident leading to death at age 70

YLL = 80 -70 = 10

Since, there’s no life lost due to disability, YLD = 0

Therefore, DALYs = YLL + YLD = 10 + 0 = 10 years

Example 3:

Life Expectancy = 80 years

Contracted AIDs at age 36.

Started medication after 4 years, i.e., at age 40

Lives up to age 70 before death.

Disability Weight for full blown AIDs without medication = 0.5

Disability Weight for AIDs with medication = 0.167

YLL = 80–70 =10

Years spent with AIDs without medication = 4

Years spent with AIDs with medication = 70–40 = 30

YLD = Years Lost Due to AIDs without Medication + Years Lost Due to AIDs with medication

= (4 * 0.5) + (30 * 0.167) = 2 + 5 = 7

DALYs = YLL + YLD = 10 + 7 = 17

Now, imagine how high the DALYs of diarrhea that affects kids will be due to years of life lost.

As at 2008 according to WHO, Diarrhea causes 52.5 million DALYs per year, which is 3.1% of the global total and 9% of child disease burden, with my dearest country😂, Nigeria standing tall at the number 3 on the list with 3.9 million DALYs.

Remember how I mentioned earlier that diarrheal diseases are water-borne diseases caused by pathogens? There are different classes of pathogens such as Protozoa, Bacteria, Viruses, and Helminths with the first three being the most important.

Classes of Pathogens

The first thing to note is that pathogens are very small, much more smaller than the human hair which is about 0.1 millimeter (mm) or 100 microns (µm) in diameter.

1. Protozoa: The largest class of pathogens with a size of 10–50 µm and are one-celled eukaryotes i.e. the cells have nucleus. Some protozoa form an egg-like cyst to survive harsh conditions such as extreme temperature, chemicals or prolonged periods without food and water. Many protozoa are parasites and cause diseases like malaria and gardia.

Entomoeba histolytica and cryptosporidium parvum are causes of severe diarrhea with the former causing amoebic dysentery/ bloody diarrhea which affects more adults than children and the latter commonly called crypto 😂 is the leading cause of diarrhea in children. Crypto is the most commonly isolated pathogen after rotavirus, forming cysts of about 5 µm in diameter which are highly resistant to treatment with even chlorine having no effect on it. It is also a major cause of deaths among HIV/AIDs patients. The infectious dose (the amount needed to cause disease) for Crypto and other protozoa is low, even a single cyst can cause disease.

2. Bacteria: Unlike protozoa, bacteria have prokaryotic cells i.e. the cells do not contain nucleus. Bacteria are few µm in size, have varying shape such as spheres, rods, or spirals and can be found everywhere, in the soil, deep ocean and even acidic hot springs with a gram of soil or milliliter of water containing several millions of bacterial cells. The vast majority of which are harmless or even beneficial to humans. However, few like E.coli, Vibrio Cholera cause diseases such as cholera, trachoma or salmonella. Like most bacteria, E.coli is about 1–2 µm in size and is universally found in human and animal faeces but isn’t normally pathogenic, in fact it is the preferred indicator bacteria used to demonstrate faecal contamination.

However, some strains of E.coli called pathogenic e.coli cause diseases, of which one group is the enterotoxogenic E.coli (ETEC) which is found to be among top 5 pathogens isolated from children with diarrhea. Another one is shigella, a distant relative of e.coli. Together, both cause 1/3 of global mortality due to diarrheal diseases. Vibrio Cholera like its name is responsible for cholera which spreads very rapidly in the right conditions like places with overcrowding and poor sanitation and hygiene, and can cause severe diarrhea and death within hours if not treated. Cholera has an estimated 3–5 million cases and 100,000–200,000 deaths every year.

3. Viruses: The smallest pathogens, typically 0.1 µm (100 nanometers) or even smaller in diameter have no independent metabolism i.e. only grows on or reproduce within a living host cell and can’t multiply within the environment. Many viruses are host specific, causing diseases in humans or specific animals only. The most widespread water-borne viruses affecting humans are rotavirus and hepatitis A and E with the former being the main pathogen causing diarrheal diseases and the single most commonly isolated pathogen among children with diarrhea. It is particularly prevalent among the youngest children and infected people shed large numbers of rotavirus in their faeces.

The virus is also highly infective with only 10–100 virus particles needed to cause infection (meaning it also has low infection dose). Rotavirus is estimated to cause over 500,000 deaths each year in 2004, with more than 85% of these deaths occurring in Africa and Asia. Hepatitis A and E is spread through food, water or direct contact with infected people. Both are widely spread in the developing world in countries with poor sanitation and hygiene, with nearly all the children being infected before age 10.

Although Polio is nearly eradicated, it still remains an important water-borne virus with only 3 countries — Afghanistan, Nigeria and Pakistan remaining polio endemic.

4. Helminths/Parasitic worms: These invade human intestines or tissues with transmission mainly due to poor sanitation and hygiene. However, dracunculus medinesis (Guinea worm) is mainly transmitted through drinking water. Its larvae lives in freshwater, gets eaten by small aquatic insects called copepods, which are typically 1mm, big enough to be seen by the naked eye.

Once a person drinks water containing copepods, the hydrochloric acid in the stomach kills the insect and releases the larvae, matures into adult worms which can reach a length of nearly a meter and width of a spaghetti noodle. The worms migrate through the body and emerge through the skin often near the feet. The worm has to be removed slowly, winding it up and pulling it out of the body bit by bit over weeks, which is extremely painful and creates sores and blisters. Thankfully, because the copepods are large, guineaworm can be beaten without vaccines or drugs but through community-scale interventions which involve the protection and treatment of drinking water like using simple cloth or sand filters to readily remove them. This refers to the intervention for water-based diseases by targeting the aquatic organism host.

entry.title: Water: The Blue Gold
entry.content:
Water (H2O), a seemingly ordinary compound of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom is the lifeblood of our planet, playing an indispensable role in sustaining all forms of life and as a nearly universal solvent.

Professor Paul Westerhoff whose research on atmospheric water harvesting I enjoy so much once said “Even when you don’t see water, taste water or touch water, you’re still using water”.

The blue gold plays its valuable roles in;

  • Human Bodies: Facilitating various bodily functions, regulates body temperature and maintaining optimal hydration levels.
  • Backbone of Agriculture: Serving as the primary resource for irrigation, sustains crop growth, ensuring food security and flourishing of a vibrant ecosystem.
  • Maintains the delicate balance of the earth’s ecosystem.
  • Source of life for both terrestrial and aquatic organisms.
  • A vital medium for nutrient transport, soil erosion control and temperature regulation.
  • The wetlands (areas of land saturated or flooded with water permanently or seasonally) act as natural filters for the purification and improvement of water quality.
  • A vital resource for various industries and also a potential source of renewable energy.
As valuable as water is, its scarcity is a looming threat on the ecosystem as the number of people with access to water steadily increases.

Although, water makes up over 70% of the Earth’s surface, and 97% of this being ocean water which are salty/saline, the freshwater available for use is just 3% of this composition.

Most of the uneven distribution of freshwater around the world can be explained by the different levels of precipitation (rainfall and snow). However, climate change also has an impact on precipitation with the increase in floods and droughts that affect some areas more than the others.

You now have a glimpse to how much precious water is, so make sure to use water intently like the gold it is, remembering that many regions would cross mountains to possess that blue gold in your hands.
